extracted.intended_audience: philosophers of mathematics and practicing mathematicians interested in the nature, epistemology, and methodology of proof
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic essay on the nature, role, and epistemic function of mathematical proofs in practice, contrasting informal conceptual proofs with formal derivations and exploring methodological, social, and epistemological criteria for proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs as generators of methods and concepts
rubrics_metrics.description: The essence of mathematics resides in inventing methods, tools, strategies and concepts for solving problems; proofs do more than establish truth — they create analytic tools and catalyse further developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: attempts to prove the Goldbach conjecture led to sieve methods (Merlin → Brun) and Schnirelmann's combinatorial density ideas; efforts on the continuum hypothesis spurred topology and descriptive set theory. Thus the value of a proof/attempt is measured by methodological innovation and research catalysis, not only by the 'truth-value' of the conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between conceptual proofs and formal derivations
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'proof' (informal, conceptual, meaning-bearing) is different from a 'derivation' (a syntactic object in a formal system); proofs have irreducible semantic content while derivations are purely symbolic and mechanically checkable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivations are finite sequences of formulas checked mechanically; conceptual proofs include meanings, context and technical understanding that cannot in general be recovered from a formal derivation. Hilbert's Thesis (that every conceptual proof can be converted into a formal derivation) is questioned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanatory and meaning-dependent content of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality proof uses meanings, background theory, conceptual understanding and methodological reasoning rather than merely citing rules of formal logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mathematical papers typically make jumps 'as is well known' or refer to background theorems; understanding often requires interpolating many intermediate claims using domain knowledge. Logical rules play a role but are usually implicit; appreciating a proof demands subject-matter expertise and contextual knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological novelty requirement for solving hard problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Solving certain problems requires genuinely new methods or conceptual moves rather than new rules of logic; proofs are valued for introducing new ways to approach problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert's remark: the continuum problem's solution requires new ways, since old methods fail; thus the standard of adequacy for a proof includes whether it provides new tools or avenues of research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infinitary and open-ended character of proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs (as understood in practice) can be infinitary in character: the process of interpolating intermediate steps may have no theoretical upper bound and what counts as 'sufficiently explained' can vary by agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The need to insert sequences A → A1 → A2 → ... → B to justify a claim can be unbounded; philosophers (Brouwer, Zermelo, Kreisel) emphasize this aspect. Acceptability of gaps depends on the reader's skill, background and community standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of non-axiomatised mathematical practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Many substantial areas of mathematics are not presented as fully axiomatized theories, yet produce rigorous and valuable results; axiomatizability is not a necessary criterion for mathematical worth or correctness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include matrix theory, graph theory, probability and number theory which historically and practically developed without being reduced to neat axiom sets; the practice of mathematics often operates beyond formal axiomatic presentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs contribute to systemic cohesiveness and theory-building
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs are judged by their ability to link theories, systematise knowledge and provide a coherent body of concepts and methods (termed 'systemic cohesiveness').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A proof's epistemic content goes beyond the isolated theorem: it organizes concepts, reveals connections between domains (e.g., topology, set theory, number theory) and thereby enhances the coherence of mathematical knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social validation and communal cross-checks
rubrics_metrics.description: The reliability of mathematical proofs arises from social processes: sharing ideas, criticism, independent checking and community consensus are central to accepting proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Computer-formalization is not the primary source of reliability; instead the human process of critique and independent verification (peer review, replication of arguments) weeds out errors. References: DeMillo–Lipton–Perlis, Thurston.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic and heuristic criteria (beauty, harmony, tool-making)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians are guided by aesthetic considerations—beauty, harmony and elegance—which play a role in evaluating and choosing proofs and research directions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author characterizes mathematicians as artisans/artists (Homo faber) guided by beauty; aesthetic judgment influences what methods are pursued and valued, though it is not reducible to formal correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits and epistemic shortcomings of formal verification
rubrics_metrics.description: Complete formalisation and machine verification of mainstream informal proofs is practically and epistemically limited: formalisation is costly, risks losing semantic elements, and probabilistic verification does not replace human understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Babai's observation: theorem-candidates need enormous formal appendices (definitions, notation, axioms like ZF, implementation of logic). Even with probabilistic checking, results would be 'probably true' in a technical sense; thus formal checking cannot capture all epistemic roles of proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logic supplies deductive skeleton but not full explanatory content
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of logic provide the formal inferential backbone of proofs, but they are insufficient to produce the explanatory, conceptual and methodological content that mathematicians rely on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No new inference rules are needed for new problems; mathematicians do not reason by citing formal rules but by informal consequences, known theorems and techniques. Thus assessment of proofs must look beyond raw inferential validity to explanatory power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of innovative (even abortive) proof attempts
rubrics_metrics.description: An attempted proof that fails formally may nonetheless be valuable if it introduces new ideas or methods; incorrect derivations without innovation are epistemically barren.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Merlin's invalid proofs of Goldbach were the seed for Brun's sieve — the abortive attempt had methodological fruit. The distinction between a mere incorrect derivation and an innovative but incomplete proof is crucial in evaluating contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability thresholds depend on agent and community standards
rubrics_metrics.description: How much justification or interpolation a proof requires before being accepted depends on the agent's background and on communal norms; there is no absolute atomic unit of justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'arrow interpolations' modelled as dialogues: different interlocutors demand different lengths and depths of justification. This subjectivity is handled by communal practices and education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofs as displays and justifications of problem-solving machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: A proof should display the mathematical machinery used to solve a problem and justify that the solution indeed resolves the posed question; proofs are the means by which problem-solving techniques are presented and assessed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The term 'problem' covers conjectures, structure-charting, and application-driven questions. Good proofs clarify methods, assumptions, and how conclusions follow from premises, enabling others to apply or extend those methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and implicit appeal to higher-order reasoning in mainstream proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Mainstream mathematical practice often relies implicitly on second-order or higher-order reasoning and concepts that are not capturable within a complete and effective first-order deductive system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: many standard theorems in group theory or concepts like 'finite group' are expressed or understood in a way that goes beyond first-order formalizability; this limits the scope of strictly first-order formal verification as a standard of practice.
